opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, because when I first looked at those early works, the core of them was still a vision problem. You take an image or a depth map, you run a network over it, and you predict where the gripper should go: a grasp pose, maybe a rectangle in the image, maybe a 6-DoF pose in 3D. Structurally, that's very close to detection or pose estimation. The "robotics" part was mostly a fixed pipeline afterward: plan a path, move there, close the gripper, lift.

So from my perspective as someone coming from 3D vision, it felt like we had just changed the label. Instead of labeling a bounding box for a cup, you label where you can grab the cup. The network architectures were similar and the training paradigm was similar. And the evaluation was often static: did you predict a good grasp on this point cloud?

What was missing was the part that makes robotics fundamentally different, which is interaction and closed-loop feedback. In vision, you observe the world and you're done. In robotics, your action changes the world, and then you have to observe again and react. Early grasping mostly treated it as a single-shot perception problem: look once, decide once, execute open-loop. It didn't really deal with contact, with dynamics, with what happens when the object slips or the scene is cluttered and things move when you touch them.

Also, grasping by itself is a very narrow slice of manipulation. Picking something up is the beginning of a task, not the task. What you really care about is what you do after: opening a drawer, folding cloth, using a tool, handing something to a person. Those require sequential decisions and an understanding of physics and affordances over time. Early grasping didn't touch that.

So my feeling was: this is useful, it's real progress, but it's not yet a new paradigm. It's vision extended slightly into action. The exciting departure only comes when the network is actually responsible for the behavior: closing the loop, handling contact-rich interaction, generalizing across tasks. That's where you're really doing embodied intelligence rather than vision with a robot arm attached at the end.

r001.rationale: The response describes predicting grasp poses from images or depth maps and evaluating predictions on point clouds, but it does not clearly characterize this as 3D geometric inference about which geometry is graspable.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes early grasping as “look once, decide once, execute open-loop,” with no ongoing feedback.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I first started working on grasping with deep learning, around 2016 or so, the whole thing felt very much like a vision problem wearing a robotics costume. You take an RGB-D image, you feed it into a network, and the network outputs a grasp pose, maybe a rectangle on the image, maybe a 6-DoF pose. Then you execute it with an open-loop controller. The robot itself is almost an afterthought. If you squint, it's just object detection where the label happens to be "where to put the gripper."

And that's exactly why it didn't feel like a departure. The data pipeline was the same as vision: collect images, annotate them, train, evaluate on a held-out set. The architectures were borrowed wholesale from detection and segmentation. Even the metrics were vision-flavored. People reported accuracy on grasp rectangles against a benchmark like Cornell, which is basically an IoU threshold. Whether the physical grasp actually succeeded was almost secondary.

What was missing was everything that makes robotics hard. There was no notion of contact, no closed loop, no reasoning about what happens after the fingers touch the object. You predicted a pose from a single frame and then hoped. Real manipulation is a process. The object moves, your perception was slightly off, the gripper slips. None of that was in the learning problem. So the "robot" part was really just a verification step at the end.

I think that's also why many people in the vision community looked at it and thought, well, this is just an application. And in a sense they were right. The intellectual content was in the perception. The interaction, the dynamics, the fact that the robot's own actions change what it will see next, that's what should have made it a different field, and in those early years it just wasn't there yet.

What changed my view later was realizing that the interesting structure in grasping isn't in the image at all. It's in the geometry and the physics. Once you start thinking in terms of 3D point clouds, contact models, and policies that can correct themselves, the problem stops looking like vision and starts looking like something genuinely new.

r001.rationale: The response mentions point clouds, geometry, and physics, but does not explain that direct grasp prediction from a point cloud reduces the task to inferring which geometry is graspable.

r002.rationale: It describes predicting a grasp from a single observation and executing it with an open-loop controller, without ongoing feedback.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason was that we were still treating grasping largely as a perception problem. You take an RGB image or a depth image, feed it into a neural network, and predict a grasp pose or score a set of grasp candidates. Then the robot executes that prediction, often with a fairly fixed controller.

So the learning problem looked very familiar from computer vision: instead of predicting a bounding box, you were predicting where the gripper should go. That was useful, but it didn’t really capture what makes robotics interesting to me—the interaction. The robot acts, the object moves, contact changes, and the robot needs to respond. If you reduce all of that to a prediction from a single image, it can feel more like extending computer vision than learning how to act in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response describes predicting a grasp from RGB or depth images, but it does not mention point clouds or explain grasping as a 3D geometric inference problem about graspable geometry.

r002.rationale: It says the robot executes a grasp predicted from a single image, often with a fixed controller, and contrasts that with responding to interaction and contact changes. This communicates execution without ongoing feedback.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason was that we were still treating grasping as a computer vision problem. You take an image or a point cloud, feed it into a neural network, and predict a grasp pose or score some grasp candidates. The robot then executes that prediction. So although the output is an action, the formulation feels very similar to object detection: instead of predicting a bounding box, you predict where the gripper should go.

That’s useful, but it doesn’t fully capture what makes robotics interesting—the interaction. When you touch an object, it can move; contact gives you new information; and you may need to adjust your action. If all of that is reduced to a single prediction from a static observation, it doesn’t feel like a fundamentally different problem from vision.

r001.rationale: The response says a point cloud is used to predict a grasp pose or score candidates, but it does not explain this as 3D geometric inference about which geometry is graspable.

r002.rationale: It describes predicting from a static observation and then having the robot execute that prediction, with no ongoing feedback.
